column3: BSB renders “Timothy the brother” as “Timothy our brother” and joins “beloved and fellow worker” into “beloved fellow worker,” dropping the Greek “and” (καί) between the two titles.
BSB adds “that meets” to “the church at your house” (κατ᾽ οἶκόν σου) and supplies “our” before “sister”; the Greek says “the sister.” LSV’s “the beloved” follows the Textus Receptus (ἀγαπητῇ).
BSB moves “to you” after “grace and peace”; the Greek greeting has no verb and reads “Grace to you and peace.”
“Remembering you” renders μνείαν σου ποιούμενος (“making mention of you”). In Greek, “always” (πάντοτε) can go with either “I thank” or “making mention.”
BSB reverses the Greek order (“your love and the faith”) and gives each noun its own object. The Greek has one relative clause: “which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.”
BSB adds “I pray” and renders εἰς Χριστόν (“toward/for Christ”) as “in Christ.” “Every good thing that is ours” renders ἐν ἡμῖν (“in us”); the Textus Receptus reads “in you” (ὑμῖν).
The Greek past tense “I had much joy” (ἔσχον) appears as present “I take great joy.” σπλάγχνα (“inner parts, affections”) is rendered “hearts.”
Close to the Greek. The participle “having much boldness” becomes a concessive clause (“although … I am bold enough”).
BSB splits the verse and renders πρεσβύτης as “aged”; some read it as “ambassador” (πρεσβευτής). “Being such a one as Paul” is restructured into “For I, Paul, am.”
BSB paraphrases “whom I begot in my chains” as “whose father I became” and moves “Onesimus” forward; in Greek the name comes last.
BSB adds “he has become.” The Greek is a verbless contrast, “once useless to you, but now useful,” a play on the name Onesimus (“useful”).
BSB renders τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα (“my own inner parts”) as “my very heart.” Like the critical text, it has no “receive him” (προσλαβοῦ), which appears in the Textus Receptus.
Close to the Greek. “I would have liked” renders the imperfect ἐβουλόμην (“I was wishing”), and BSB adds “my” and “for” to “the chains of the gospel.”
BSB renders τὸ ἀγαθόν σου (“your good”) as “your goodness” and κατὰ ἑκούσιον (“according to willingness”) as “by your own free will.”
BSB adds “from you” and “back”; πρὸς ὥραν is literally “for an hour,” and αἰώνιον (“eternally”) is rendered “for good.”
BSB splits the verse and adds “He is”; ἐν σαρκί (“in the flesh”) is rendered “in person.”
“Consider me a partner” renders με ἔχεις κοινωνόν (“you have me as a partner”); “as you would receive me” expands “as me.”
Close to the Greek; “charge this to me” (ἐμοὶ ἐλλόγα) becomes “charge it to my account.”
BSB renders the epistolary aorist ἔγραψα (“I wrote”) as present “I write,” and “that I may not say to you” as “not to mention.”
“Let me have some benefit” renders the wish ὀναίμην (“may I have profit”), a play on the name Onesimus. “Heart” renders σπλάγχνα.
BSB renders the aorist ἔγραψα as present “I write,” and “beyond what I say” as “even more than I ask.”
“A guest room” renders ξενία (“lodging, hospitality”). “I will be restored to you” renders χαρισθήσομαι ὑμῖν (“I will be granted to you as a gift”).
Close to the Greek; “greets you” (ἀσπάζεταί σε) becomes “sends you greetings.”
BSB adds “as do” and “and” to connect the list to verse 23; the Greek is only a list of names.
BSB follows the critical text: “the Lord” without “our,” and no “Amen.” “Our,” “Amen,” and the closing note (“written to Philemon from Rome by Onesimus”) come from the Textus Receptus.
